designs.name: Pure callback / CPS (Node-style)
designs.summary: Write the connection layer and handler API directly in continuation-passing style over chez-libuv's existing callback shapes: every async step takes k : (err value) -> unspecified and calls it exactly once from a later libuv callback; no continuations captured, no threads, no engines. Six ~10-line combinators (cps-guard, once, cps-bind, cps-seq, cps-each, cps-while, cps-all) are the entire runtime support. The driver pauses the parser at on-message-complete so `consumed` marks message boundaries (measured: consumed=28 for a 28-byte GET, second message at offset 56), parses ahead up to a cap, and uses uv-read-stop!/uv-read-start! plus stored continuations for backpressure. Two spikes ran today: a socket-less CPS core replaying a POST body at every chunk size 1..60 with identical body and coalesced event stream, and a loopback CPS HTTP/1.1 server serving 200 pipelined requests in order (199x200 + 1x500 from a deliberate handler raise), awaiting uv-getaddrinfo! inside a handler, triggering one uv-read-stop! at cap=4, and closing exactly once. Strongest properties: zero dependence on the continuation-across-foreign-callable question, smallest surface over the binding (which is already CPS), trivially pure core (conn-step : State Event -> State x Commands), ~2.7 KB allocated per request in the core. Weakest: handler ergonomics (nested lambdas, no dynamic extent across awaits, continuation arity/exactly-once unchecked by the language — an arity slip in the spike stopped the whole loop via store-and-reraise). Full proposal with citations and verbatim outputs at the report path.
chez_assumptions: NOT relied upon: invoking a continuation captured inside a foreign-callable after that callable returned. CPS never captures one. CSUG foreign.html §4.4: 'A foreign context becomes stale after a normal return to the context or after a return to some other foreign context beneath it on the control stack' and the system is 'trapping attempts to return to stale foreign contexts'; 'the C stack pointer is not automatically restored to its base value when a continuation is used on the Scheme side to perform a nonlocal exit'. Whether a continuation captured in one callable can be resumed from another is exactly the stale-context question the live spike measures; this proposal is correct either way.

Relied upon: a guard established inside a foreign-callable that catches without escaping is safe. chez-libuv's own dispatch-guarded (handles.sls:302-304) depends on it and passes its suites; cps-guard is the same construct one level up.
Relied upon: allocation and GC inside a foreign-callable are ordinary (test-echo.sps calls (collect) inside every callback per design spec S11).

Relied upon: callbacks run only on the loop thread, one at a time; uv-run refuses re-entry from a callback (loop.sls:55-56); libuv's threadpool never runs Scheme (api.md DNS). Hence no mutex around connection state and no use of the unsynchronised handle registry from other threads. threads.html: foreign-created threads 'must call Sactivate_thread ... before touching any Scheme data' — not exercised.
Relied upon: Chez's segmented stack tolerates the pump's synchronous recursion, which is bounded by the pipelining cap anyway.
Assumed, unmeasured in isolation: a pending-step closure costs a few dozen bytes; bounded by the measured 2672 B/request.
Not used: call/1cc ('A one-shot continuation should not be returned to multiple times'), engines, fork-thread.
risks: Continuation arity and exactly-once are unchecked by the language: an arity slip (k err) vs (lambda (err v)) in the spike stopped the whole loop via store-and-reraise; a forgotten k hangs silently (only response-timeout catches it); `once` catches double calls at runtime only.

The pyramid: sequential awaits plus a streaming loop become nested lambdas or a monadic cps-seq/cps-bind pipeline; readable but foreign to most Scheme programmers; macro sugar (async-let*) helps but adds a second sub-language.

Dynamic extent does not survive a step: parameterize, with-exception-handler, dynamic-wind, current-output-port redirection do not span an await; request-scoped context must be explicit in the request record.
Stack traces stop at the trampoline; cps-guard must annotate conditions with request id and step name by hand.

Every boundary needs cps-guard; a handler passing its own lambda straight to uv-getaddrinfo! is unguarded unless it goes through an http-await proxy — one missed guard stops service for all connections.

Synchronous completion re-entrancy: a step that calls k before returning runs the rest of the pipeline inside the caller's frame; state mutated after the call sees the future (rule: never assume code after a step call runs before k).
Recursion in the pump (feed -> pump -> feed) is bounded only by the pipelining cap; a cap misconfigured to thousands would deepen the stack on a delivery full of tiny requests.
httparse does not export the F-* flag integers (grammar.sls:301-306); the server must restate llhttp's constants and pin them with a test (inherited by every proposal).

Byte-machine zero-width step after a pause on the last body byte: the driver must feed once more even with an empty range or the message never completes (runtime.sls:1144-1148); the first spike hung on it.

Where CPS is simply worse than a coroutine per connection: handler authoring ergonomics (the four points above). Where it is better: no dependence on the continuation-across-C question, zero per-request control-state cost, smallest surface over a binding that is already CPS, trivially pure core, no scheduler to test. If the live spike proves captured continuations resumable across callables, an await layer can be built on top of this driver later without changing it; the reverse is not true.

designs.name: Two-level loop with coroutines on one-shot continuations
designs.summary: A Scheme scheduler owns the top level: each turn it resumes every runnable coroutine to its next suspension point, then calls (uv-run loop 'once) — which blocks in the OS poll until libuv has something to deliver — and repeats ('nowait only when a coroutine yield!ed for fairness). libuv callbacks never run user code: each pushes an event onto a per-connection inbox or fulfils a one-shot resume cell and returns. Coroutines are call/1cc-based and every continuation is captured and invoked only in frames the scheduler entered, never inside a foreign-callable, so the open question about invoking callable-captured continuations is sidestepped by construction (checked at runtime by a scheduler 'phase' assertion). One coroutine per connection owns the parser, the inbox, the outstanding-write counters and the ordered response stream, and runs handlers in arrival order on its own stack (v2: per-request coroutines behind an ordering gate with max-pipeline-depth). Handlers are direct-style (request-read!, response-write!, await, with-deadline). Measured on this machine today: the scheduler blocked in uv-run for 402 of 402 ms across 6 uv-run calls with no busy loop; a yield/resume pair costs 24 ns and ~7 bytes (359 ns from 200 frames deep); a parked coroutine costs 3.4–5.6 KiB resident at 10k; callback-pause at on-message-complete gives an exact pipelining boundary via parser-result-consumed (51 then 47 bytes) and feeding after a Connection: close message errors with 'closed-connection; a guard inside a coroutine catches a raise that occurs after suspend/resume and an uncaught coroutine raise lands in the scheduler's plain Scheme guard. Consequence: application code can never trigger chez-libuv's store-and-reraise loop stop, because it never runs under a C frame. Full document: research/async-two-level-coroutines.md.
chez_assumptions: A1 (structural, spike-independent): a continuation captured in a Scheme frame entered from the scheduler may be invoked after intervening uv-run foreign-procedure calls have returned normally — CSUG foreign.html §4.4: 'until some return to a foreign context is actually performed, all return points remain valid', and a foreign context is a C->Scheme call, none of which exists between the scheduler and any captured k; exercised 6 times in spike/two-level.sps without incident.

A2 (the open question, deliberately NOT depended on): whether a continuation captured inside a foreign-callable may be invoked after that callable returned. CSUG §4.4 says Chez traps 'attempts to return to stale foreign contexts', so the expected outcome is a trapped error rather than corruption; this proposal never captures inside a callable (rules R1/R2, checked by the scheduler 'phase' assertion), so it is correct whichever way the live spike lands. If the spike shows it is safe, resuming coroutines directly from callbacks would be simpler than this design.

A3: one-shot promotion is transparent — if code inside a handler obtains a call/cc continuation while a coroutine is active (R6RS guard reraise, SRFI generators), the active call/1cc continuations are promoted to multishot (CSUG control.html §6.3), which is correct; measured cost difference 24 vs 29 ns, so nothing depends on staying one-shot.
A4: dynamic-wind winders run on every suspend/resume (measured in=2 out=2 for one park), so parameterize across an await is correct but re-executed; documented as an avoid-in-hot-handlers rule.

A5: no non-local exit ever crosses a C frame in this design, so CSUG §4.4's 'C stack pointer is not automatically restored' caveat does not apply; &uv-callback-error, if ever raised, is raised after uv-run returned normally.

A6: single OS thread; uv-run bound plain; __collect_safe unused (chez-libuv spike FINDINGS 'deliberately untested: __collect_safe x callback re-entry'); the handle registry is an unsynchronised eqv-hashtable (handles.sls:218).

A7: call/1cc capture/resume cost scales with the live stack segment (CSUG §6.3 cites 'Representing control in the presence of one-shot continuations'), consistent with 24 ns shallow vs 359 ns at 200 frames — handlers should await at modest depth.

A8: a coroutine must never return normally into the scheduler's already-used one-shot continuation; it must end by jumping to the scheduler's CURRENT k — violating this crashed both spikes ('Exception in +: go is not a number') and is rule R3.
risks: Discipline that must be policed at runtime, not compile time: safety rests on callbacks never running user code or capturing continuations (R1/R2) and parser callbacks never awaiting (R5); a violation surfaces as a fatal &uv-callback-error. The plain callback model has no such rule to break.

Memory: 3.4-5.6 KiB resident per parked coroutine (measured at 10k) vs ~200 B of closures in the callback model — ~35-56 MB extra at 10k connections, and those stack segments are scanned by major GCs (unmeasured under load). Smaller than the read buffer at any size >= 8 KiB, but real.

One extra hop per delivery (~24 ns switch + a cons + queue ops) and one more uv-run iteration boundary before user code sees an event — negligible against a syscall, strictly more than the callback model.

No cross-thread wakeup: uv_async is not bound by chez-libuv, so nothing can wake a scheduler blocked in uv-run 'once from another OS thread; off-loop CPU work is impossible in v1. Mitigation: request uv_async as a fourteenth locked trampoline under ADR-0008's rule.

No preemption: a CPU-bound handler starves every connection and with-deadline cannot interrupt it; engines were rejected because engine-block would capture inside parser-feed! and poison the parser. The callback model has the same property, so this is not worse, just not better.
Debugging unfamiliarity: a parked coroutine's stack is a heap object; backtraces show only its own segment.
v1 executes handlers sequentially per connection, so one slow pipelined request delays the rest; v2's per-request coroutines fix that at the cost of an ordering gate and max-pipeline-depth.

Reliance on callback-pause at three points (headers-complete, body-data, message-complete): the corpus records pauses for 24 fixtures and the spike confirmed the two needed here, but the pause path is less exercised upstream than the straight path.

The 16 KiB read-buffer recommendation was measured by chez-libuv discarding deliveries (api.md:164-171 'a consumer that retains deliveries ... was not measured'); this server retains deliveries in the inbox, so the object-count/GC cost is open.

If the live spike shows callable-captured continuations are safe to invoke later, the obvious alternative (resume coroutines directly from callbacks) needs less machinery and has lower latency; this proposal's remaining advantages are determinism (application code can never cause chez-libuv's store-and-reraise loop stop) and independence from an implementation property CSUG documents only obliquely.

designs.name: Chez engines for cooperative time-slicing
designs.summary: One engine per connection; every libuv callback is a pure event recorder (push an inbox chunk / set a flag / store a completion) that wakes the connection by a run-queue push, never by invoking a continuation; the scheduler runs engine slices in batches at the top level of the loop thread and polls with uv-run 'nowait when tasks are runnable and 'once when none are. The parser is pulled inside the engine, so parsing, handler, and response writing are all preemptible and the layer is a function from an inbox of bytevectors to writes. Measured on this machine (Chez 10.4.1): engines cannot nest ("cannot nest engines"), a blocked engine retains ~650-800 B, a block/resume round trip costs ~25 B / ~0.5 us, a tight loop is preempted at its tick limit but a C call is not, dynamic-wind thunks run at every slice boundary, and an idle uv-run 'nowait costs ~13 us (so slices must be batched per poll). A working spike ran a CPU hog, timer awaits, and a uv-getaddrinfo! await under this scheduler against real chez-libuv and tore down cleanly.
chez_assumptions: A1 (NOT relied upon; stated as required): whether a continuation captured inside a foreign-callable may be invoked after that callable returned is treated as unknown. CSUG foreign.html §4.4: 'A foreign context becomes stale after a normal return to the context or after a return to some other foreign context beneath it on the control stack.' This design captures continuations only in engine code that runs outside every callback, so it needs nothing from the live spike.
A2 (measured, Chez 10.4.1): engines cannot nest — 'Exception in engine: cannot nest engines'. The scheduler is the sole engine invoker; handlers and libraries they call must not use engines.

A3 (CSUG control.html §6.4, quoted): 'Do not use the timer interrupt (see set-timer) and engines at the same time, since engines are implemented in terms of the timer.' No set-timer/timer-interrupt-handler anywhere in server or handlers; libuv timers are C and unaffected.

A4 (CSUG system.html Interrupts, quoted; measured): interrupts are 'supported via a counter that is decremented approximately once for each call to a nonleaf procedure' — a foreign call is not preemptible (usleep(20000) x2 completed inside a 10-tick engine with 7 ticks left; a loop of usleep(0) calls was preempted).

A5 (measured): dynamic-wind after-thunks run when an engine blocks and before-thunks run on resume ((in out) after block, (in out in out) after completion); parameterize is unwound at block and restored at resume. Handlers pay wind/unwind at every slice boundary.

A6 (measured): a raise inside an engine propagates to the engine's invoker and consumes the engine; new engines work afterwards; a guard inside the engine keeps it alive — hence guards live inside run-handler! and at run-slice!.
A7 (measured once, not documented): engine-block from a nested Scheme call works; call/1cc captured before a block and invoked after resume worked here but handlers are told not to rely on it.

A8 (assumed): engine/timer-interrupt state is per-thread and the loop runs on exactly one thread; chez-libuv's handle registry is unsynchronised and no Scheme runs on libuv worker threads (api.md DNS section).
A9 (measured): (collect) inside an engine and 10k allocation-heavy engines leave engine accounting intact.
A10 (CSUG §6.4, quoted): tick-to-time mapping is unspecified ('Your mileage may vary'), so slice-ticks is a benchmarked config knob, not a constant.
risks: Worse than a pure callback/CPS connection state machine for trivial handlers: engines add a scheduler and a ~13 us poll to amortise while buying nothing until a handler blocks or hogs.

Worse than one-shot coroutines (call/1cc yield-at-await) if handlers are trusted: same direct-style API without the nesting restriction, dynamic-wind churn, or timer-interrupt coupling; engines only win when preemption is a requirement.
The no-nesting restriction is a user-facing footgun: any handler or library using engines fails at runtime (contained as a 500, not fixable by the server).
Poll latency vs throughput tension in batch-max/slice-ticks must be settled by benchmark; too small wastes 13 us per slice, too large delays accepts and reads under saturation.
dynamic-wind/parameterize costs are invisible to handler authors and scale with slice frequency (request-context parameters and loggers pay twice per slice).
Foreign calls are not preemptible: a slow C routine or blocking libc call stalls the loop like in every single-threaded design, and the tick count can mislead (7 ticks left after 40 ms).

Preemption can land mid parser-feed! (parser lifecycle 'busy); correct only while nothing outside the engine touches that parser — a future timer-side parser inspection would break it; guarded by a test, not a comment.
Parked-engine size grows with handler stack depth (652 -> 804 B at 30 frames); bounded in practice, unbounded in principle.

The A1 unknown is avoided rather than answered: if the live spike shows callback-captured continuations are safe, designs resuming handlers directly in on-data skip a queue hop and a slice that this design keeps for determinism (~1 us).
Windows (deferred): uv-stream-write-queue-size semantics invert, so the gauge threshold must be per-platform or disabled.
Wheel resolution of 1 s makes deadlines fire up to one tick late; sub-second deadlines need a smaller configurable tick.
The 64 KiB read-buffer default (625 MiB at 10k) is the largest number in the design; 16 KiB is proposed but is a tradeoff chez-libuv deliberately left to consumers.

The feasibility spike exercised timers and DNS but not TCP reads/writes under the scheduler; the read/write backpressure paths are designed from the API contract and test-echo.sps, not yet measured end to end.

designs.name: OS-thread worker pool for handlers, single loop thread for I/O, mutex/condition mailboxes
designs.summary: One loop thread (main) owns uv-run, every handle, the unsynchronised registry, the connection table, the timing wheel AND every parser; N = cores worker threads (fork-thread) run handlers on fully materialised request records and send commands (respond/start/write/end/read-more/close/loop-call) back through a loop-owned inbox. Parser stays on the loop thread because a full 25-callback parse costs 1.86 us/request (spike E) versus 3.9 us for a mailbox round trip (spike C), and because backpressure decisions (read-stop, callback-pause) happen inside parser callbacks and must run on the loop thread; body spans are handed to workers as (bv from to) of the fresh per-delivery bytevector with no second copy. Decisive measurement: with the loop thread blocked in chez-libuv's plain (non-__collect_safe) uv-run and nothing due, a worker that merely allocates stalls until the loop returns to Scheme — 3005 ms in spike A — because Chez's collector rendezvous cannot complete while a thread is active in C (CSUG 4.9). Tier 1 (works today): a repeating heartbeat timer (1 ms while busy, 50 ms idle) that both drains the inbox and bounds the GC stall; cost ~1% idle CPU, 573 us mean handoff. Tier 2 (recommended upstream chez-libuv v0.6 prerequisite): bind uv_async (14th locked trampoline 'async', (uptr)->void) as the one any-thread verb, and re-bind uv_run __collect_safe with all trampolines __collect_safe; spike B shows this works on raw libuv (2000/2000 fires exact under (collect), close delivered, uv_loop_close=0) and cuts the worker stall from 3001 ms to 1 ms; spike D shows uv_async_send from a Scheme worker gives 13 us mean handoff at ~0.1% idle CPU. Thread-per-request is rejected on measured cost: ~244-250 KiB RSS and ~800 KiB Scheme-heap allocation per forked thread (spike C). Strictly one in-flight request per connection gives response ordering; max-pipeline enforced by callback-pause at on-message-begin; process-wide cap via a job-queue limit answered 503 by the loop thread. Full report with every command, output and quotation: /private/tmp/claude-501/-Users-yuzu-github-chez-http-server/2440228f-3288-4faf-9838-18f1bc1cd3d2/scratchpad/research/async-threads-mailbox.md
chez_assumptions: A1 (measured): Chez 10.4.1 here is a threaded build — (threaded?) => #t, machine-type tarm64osx, collect-trip-bytes 8388608.

A2 (CSUG 4.9, measured in spike A): a thread active inside a plain foreign-procedure call (uv_run blocked in kqueue) prevents every other thread from collecting; a worker's allocation stalled 3005 ms until the loop thread's next callback. The design therefore needs either a heartbeat timer or a __collect_safe uv_run.

A3 (CSUG 4.2/4.3, measured in spike B on raw libuv, darwin/arm64 only): uv_run bound __collect_safe with every callable bound __collect_safe re-enters correctly under GC pressure (2000/2000 fires, close delivered, uv_loop_close 0) and removes the stall (1 ms vs 3001 ms). NOT yet in chez-libuv; FINDINGS.md names it as the untested gap; Linux must be re-measured in CI before tier 2 ships.

A4 (CSUG ch.15, 4.9): fork-thread threads start active; record field mutators, set-car!, vector-set! are thread-safe but hashtables are not; the design nevertheless reads/writes every shared field only under with-mutex and waits only with condition-wait + timeout (returns #f on timeout). Chez documents primitive thread-safety, not a memory model for unsynchronised set! visibility, so unsynchronised sharing is forbidden by rule.

A5 (CSUG 15.1): thread-join waits for completion; there is NO thread cancel in Chez, so a wedged handler permanently loses a pool slot; engines are built on the timer interrupt (CSUG 6.4) and are not used to bound handlers in v1.

A6 (assumption, not relied on): whether a continuation captured inside a foreign-callable may be invoked after that callable returned is left to the separate live spike; this design captures no continuation inside any libuv callback and workers block with condition-wait, so it is insensitive to that result either way. CSUG 4.4 states continuations may throw through mixed Scheme/foreign frames, but ADR-0008/FINDINGS Q2 show escapes leave invisible cleanup obligations, which is a second reason not to use them.

A7 (measured, spike D): uv_async_send called through a plain foreign-procedure from a fork-thread'd Scheme worker wakes a loop blocked in a __collect_safe uv_run; libuv coalesces sends, so the inbox is drained to empty per wake. uv_stop from another thread neither wakes the poll nor is thread-safe (observed); never called off the loop thread.
A8 (measured, spike C): an idle forked thread costs ~244-250 KiB RSS and ~800 KiB Scheme-heap allocation; a mutex/condition round trip is ~3.9 us. Pool, not thread-per-request.

A9 (ADR-0009, handles.sls:405): on-data's bytevector is fresh per delivery and never mutated afterwards, so (bv from to) triples may be shared with a worker without copying; the parser's span callbacks index that same bytevector because the loop thread feeds it directly.

A10 (CSUG 15.8): thread parameters are inherited by value at fork; per-worker state uses make-thread-parameter; thread-preserve-ownership! is available as a parallel-collection hint for workers (unmeasured).
risks: Needs an upstream chez-libuv change to be good: without uv_async and a __collect_safe uv_run the loop must poll (latency >= heartbeat period, ~1% idle CPU) and every worker's GC waits on that poll. The raw-libuv spikes show the change is small and works on darwin/arm64, but it is a v0.6 slice with its own ADR (14th trampoline, first any-thread verb, __collect_safe re-binding of uv_run and all thirteen trampolines, the frozen thirteen-name test literals widened and watched to fail) and it has not been measured on Linux.

Simply worse than the single-threaded loop for cheap or I/O-bound handlers: two mailbox hops (~4 us) plus a wake per request, and stop-the-world GC across N+1 threads. The angle only pays when handlers burn CPU or call blocking foreign code; with an unknown workload the single-thread design is the safer default (the build order keeps HTTP_WORKERS=0 as an inline-handler fallback).
Stop-the-world GC across threads means parallel handlers scale sublinearly if they allocate heavily; not measured under load.

Unkillable handlers: Chez has no thread cancel; the 'handler timeout aborts the connection and marks the request aborted so the worker unwinds at its next blocking call, but a spinning or foreign-blocked handler holds its slot forever (lost-workers metric only).

Blocked writers wedge the pool: a worker parked in response-write! behind a slow client holds a slot; max-blocked-writers aborts connections to protect the pool, a worse client experience than a single-threaded server that parks nothing.

Nondeterministic tests for the pool/inbox/wakeup half; mitigated by injecting wake!, iteration caps, sentinel symbols and a fake thunk-runner loop, but the mutation lane for this half is harder to make go red by name.
Memory-model discipline is by rule, not by the language: every shared field must be touched only under with-mutex; a reviewer lint is proposed but a slip would be a silent race.

Per-connection memory is dominated by the 64 KiB foreign read buffer, identical for every angle; the proposal sets 16 KiB by default from api.md's measurements, which is a bulk-upload throughput tradeoff not measured here.
uv-stream-write-queue-size has opposite semantics on Windows (api.md), so it is used only as a signal; Windows is deferred anyway.

The spike measurements are single-machine (macOS arm64, 8 cores); the GC-interlock behaviour is documented Chez semantics but the magnitudes (3.9 us hop, 13 us async handoff, 250 KiB/thread) should be re-measured on the Linux CI host before they are used as thresholds.

designs.name: Promise/future combinators over callbacks, with optional one-shot-continuation await
designs.summary: Two tiers. Tier 0: a ~200-line promise library (then/catch/finally/all/race/any, cooperative cancellation, timeouts on a per-server timer wheel) whose reactions are queued on a microtask FIFO drained by `with-step` inside the libuv callback that settled them, before control returns to C; no threads, engines, uv_async, or scheduler beyond that FIFO, and no Chez assumption beyond what chez-libuv already makes. The whole connection driver (functional core emitting actions with opaque settle/reject tags; imperative shell mapping libuv callbacks to events and actions to verbs/promises) is written in Tier 0. Tier 1: `spawn`/`await` built on `call/1cc` captured inside a libuv callback and resumed from a later one, under one rule: every suspension and completion escapes to the *dynamically current* callback root and never returns normally into the frames of the callback that captured it (CSUG foreign.html stale-foreign-context rule). Measured today: 1000 capture-in-A/resume-in-B rounds with a collect each, loop ran dry, teardown clean; ~120-150 ns per suspend/resume; the negative case (raise after resume with no library catch-all) reaches the stale dispatch-guarded guard and Chez traps it as a plain condition `attempt to return to stale foreign context` escaping uv-run, while the stored error was still delivered on the next uv-run and the loop survived. Read-side backpressure is parser pause (measured: `consumed` includes the delivered span; re-feed from `consumed` after `parser-resume!`) plus uv-read-stop!, gated by whether a `body-read!` promise is pending; write-side is a per-connection outstanding-bytes/requests count with high/low water and the write-queue gauge as supplemental signal, expressed as `sink-write!` promise resolution; response ordering under pipelining is a per-response `ready` promise. Errors: handler raises become rejections (never reach dispatch-guarded); parser/policy errors map to 4xx+close; transport errors reject all pending tags; only driver bugs reach store-and-reraise. Testable without sockets by replaying the llhttp corpus through the core at every chunk size and asserting chunk-invariance of request records and action streams. Report: /private/tmp/claude-501/-Users-yuzu-github-chez-http-server/2440228f-3288-4faf-9838-18f1bc1cd3d2/scratchpad/research/async-promise-combinators.md
chez_assumptions: A1: A one-shot continuation captured inside a foreign-callable body may be invoked after that callable returned to C, provided the resumed computation never returns normally to the stale foreign context and leaves by invoking another continuation (CSUG foreign.html: 'Programs that use continuations more generally also function properly as long as they never actually return to a stale foreign context, even if control logically moves past stale foreign contexts via invocation of continuations'). My own measurement today (1000 A->B rounds with collect, tarm64osx) is consistent; the separate live spike is authoritative; if it fails, Tier 1 (await) is dropped and the then-form driver is unchanged.

A2: Returning to a stale foreign context is trapped as a raise of an ordinary condition, not undefined behaviour (CSUG: 'Scheme handles this interaction in a general manner by trapping attempts to return to stale foreign contexts'; observed message 'attempt to return to stale foreign context', loop survived, teardown ok).

A3: The exception-handler stack ($current-handler-stack, a parameter) and dynamic-wind winders travel with a captured continuation and are reinstated on resume (observed: the capturing callback's dispatch-guarded guard caught a post-resume raise). Hence the library's catch-all must be the innermost handler around every resumed body.

A4: call/1cc per CSUG control.html: 'A one-shot continuation should not be returned to multiple times, either by invoking the continuation or returning normally from procedure more than once' and it is promoted to multishot if call/cc runs while it is active; Chez guard expands to call/cc (s/exceptions.ss), so guard inside a coroutine promotes the root (measured cost negligible). Handler code that re-enters a resumed body via its own call/cc is unsupported ('attempt to invoke shot one-shot continuation').

A5: Single loop thread; the promise library, microtask FIFO, wheel and chez-libuv's registry are single-thread by construction (CSUG threads.html: destructive operators are thread safe only on distinct objects); DNS completions arrive on the loop thread (docs/api.md).

A6: Memory retained by a suspended coroutine is its stack segment from the capturing callback's entry to the await point; segment size and Chez's segment allocation policy were not measured, and bytes-allocated may not count them.
A7: Engines are not used (CSUG: engines are implemented with the timer interrupt) and an engine block inside a foreign-callable would be a stale-context return by another name.

A8: uv-run's dynamic-wind thunks (loop.sls:60-63, set-loop-running!) are idempotent, so resuming across separate uv-run calls in a 'once-driven test harness is harmless; the driver must add no non-idempotent dynamic-wind or parameterize around a step.
risks: The microtask FIFO is a scheduler in miniature; the 'no scheduler' claim is only honest about threads/engines/timeslicing. It is required for parser re-entrancy safety, so it cannot be removed.

Tier 1 (await) rests entirely on assumption A1; if the live spike fails, the ergonomic advantage shrinks to then-chains, which read worse in Scheme than in JS. The design survives (all four sketches have then forms) but the pitch does not.

Stale-foreign-context traps are one escaped raise away: any path letting a condition reach the capturing callback's dispatch-guarded guard reproduces the measured failure. The catch-all must be library-owned and innermost; user code capturing full continuations inside handlers is a trap. Plain callbacks cannot have this bug class.

Swallowed errors: a rejection with no reaction is silent by default; the unhandled-rejection-hook fires only at drain end and can report spuriously when a reaction is attached in a later step (JS has the same wart). Callbacks make the error path explicit at every site.
One promise record per write on the hot path (~28 B, ~20 ns measured) plus a reaction closure; a callback design allocates the closure anyway, so the delta is small but nonzero.
Cancellation is cosmetic for writes (uv_write cannot be cancelled once submitted, ADR-0018); only DNS has a real cancel via uv-cancel!.
Debuggability: a resumed coroutine's continuation chain contains frames of a long-finished callback; inspector output is confusing. Then-chains have the opposite problem (no chain).
Memory of suspended coroutines at 10k connections is unmeasured (A6).
dynamic-wind/parameterize around a step is a contributor footgun: values are silently wrong after a resume across uv-run calls.
Windows: the write-queue gauge inverts meaning (kernel-accepted overlapped sends), so queue-high-water needs per-platform calibration; Windows is deferred anyway (ADR-0004).

Where the obvious alternative is simply better: a server whose handlers are all synchronous gains nothing and pays the FIFO, the rejection-reporting wart and the per-write promise; CPU-bound handlers are helped by no angle without preemption, and threads cannot touch the loop because uv_async is not bound.
The measured bytes-allocated for continuation cycles (13-28 B) is implausibly low and should not be quoted as the cost of a suspension until segment allocation is accounted for.

designs.name: Sans-I/O connection state machine with an action interpreter
designs.summary: The HTTP connection is a pure function conn-step : State x Event -> State x [Action]. Events are everything the world tells a connection (bytes-arrived, eof, read-error, write-completed, tick, the 25 chez-httparse callbacks as parser-event, the parser-feed! result as parser-result, handler-responded/handler-body-chunk/body-credit/handler-failed, shutdown-requested); actions are everything it asks for (reply-parser, feed-parser, resume-parser, write, read-stop, read-start, call-handler, deliver-body, notify-producer, arm-deadline, shutdown, close, log). The shell is a ~120-line interpreter: libuv callbacks build events; parser callbacks build parser-events synchronously inside parser-feed! and return the step's reply-parser action (continue/pause/skip-body/(fail code)); all other actions are queued and executed only after the outermost dispatch returns (run-to-completion), which is forced by byte-machine's non-re-entrant, escape-poisoning parser and chez-libuv's refusal of uv-run re-entry. A runnable prototype in the scratchpad runs the SAME core (a) under a socket-free fake loop: 13/13 checks including identical wire bytes at every chunk size 1..135 for the llhttp pipelining fixture, LIFO handler responses written in request order, a pipeline cap that pauses the parser+stops reads then resumes+feeds the retained remainder+restarts reads, Connection: close then more data (second request never fed; the parser's closed-connection error at offset 47 ignored), HTTP/1.0, handler raise -> 500, parser error -> 400+close, EOF with a request in flight; and (b) under a real chez-libuv loop over loopback: four pipelined requests, handlers answering 4,3,2,1 via uv timers and uv-getaddrinfo!, wire order 1,2,3,4, Connection: close honoured, connection table empty. Measured allocation: 6,832 B/request naive pure core, 14,054 B/request core+adapter+parser+fake shell. Zero continuations, zero threads, zero timer handles per connection (one per-loop tick + timing wheel; uv_timer_t measured 152 B). Full report with commands, verbatim outputs and file:line citations at the report_path.
chez_assumptions: A1: every chez-libuv callback (tcp, timer, DNS completion, signal) runs on the loop thread inside uv-run (quickstart: 'Callbacks run here and nowhere else'; api.md DNS: 'completions are delivered on the loop thread like every other callback'), so connection cells need no locks and respond is loop-thread-only.

A2: this design captures NO continuation inside any foreign-callable; whether a continuation captured inside a foreign-callable may be invoked after that callable returned is therefore NOT load-bearing. CSUG 10 §4.4 (quoted in the report): Chez 'trapping attempts to return to stale foreign contexts rather than by restricting the use of continuations directly'; 'A foreign context becomes stale after a normal return to the context'; 'programs that use continuations exclusively for nonlocal exits never attempt to return to a stale foreign context'. My reading is that such a re-entry is trapped as an error rather than silently corrupting; the separate live spike measures it and the design works under either outcome.

A3: guard/raise inside a callback is an ordinary nonlocal exit within one foreign context and is safe (CSUG §4.4: 'Nonlocal exits themselves are no problem and are implemented by the C library function longjmp or the equivalent'); used in every executor arm and by chez-libuv's own dispatch-guarded.

A4: call/1cc is not used; if a coroutine layer were added on top, CSUG §6.3 applies: 'A one-shot continuation should not be returned to multiple times' and it is 'promoted' to multishot if call/cc captures while it is active.

A5: engines are not used and would conflict with any set-timer use (CSUG §6.4: 'Do not use the timer interrupt (see set-timer) and engines at the same time, since engines are implemented in terms of the timer').

A6: libuv threadpool workers never run Scheme (api.md DNS: 'pure C; no Scheme ever runs off the loop thread'), so no Sactivate_thread question arises; threaded build assumed only so fork-thread remains available to a future uv_async bridge (CSUG foreign.html: threads not created by fork-thread 'must ... be activated before it can access Scheme data').

A7: dynamic-wind is R6RS dynamic-wind (CSUG control.html), which is what byte-machine relies on to poison a parser after a callback escape (runtime.sls:1021-1057); hence no executor ever runs inside a parser callback.
A8: parser-feed!/parser-finish!/parser-resume! are non-re-entrant (byte-machine runtime.sls:998, :1343, :1612 'reentrancy' arms), hence the run-to-completion action queue.
A9: (sstats-bytes (statistics)) is cumulative allocation (used for the per-request numbers); bytes-allocated is not (went negative across a GC in the first attempt).
A10: uv-now (cached once per loop iteration) is adequate for deadline arithmetic at tick granularity.

A11: chez-libuv's on-data bytevector is fresh per delivery and never reused by the binding (ADR-0009), so retaining it as pending-input across callbacks is safe; if a future zero-copy borrowed-span variant ships, pending-input must copy.
risks: Indirection tax: every effect is a datum interpreted elsewhere and the synchronous-reply vs deferred-effect split adds decision points; the prototype hit exactly such a bug (Connection: close decided at response arrival instead of write time), caught by the loopback test.
The interpreter (executor) is not covered by the socket-free tests; it needs loopback tests and is kept tiny and contract-tested (same action stream -> same wire bytes in both shells).
Streaming bodies cost two conn-step round trips per chunk versus writing directly from the producer; negligible at 64 KiB chunks, not at 1 KiB.

pending-input retains the whole delivery bytevector (up to read-buffer-size) per paused connection until resume, potentially doubling the read-buffer footprint for paused connections; copying the remainder is a tunable.

Pausing inside on-body-data (credit-based upload path) relies on the resume point after a SPAN pause being exactly `to`; corpus covers 24 requested pauses at every chunk size and a body-then-pause fixture, but this exact site must be pinned by a connection-layer test before it is relied on; fallback is pausing at chunk/message boundaries with one buffered span.

Handler ergonomics are callback-style with no await; engine/continuation-based proposals will read better in handlers. Coroutines can be layered on top later, but if the live spike shows re-entry after a foreign-callable returns is not allowed, that layer needs fork-thread + uv_async (not bound).

Cross-thread handlers unsupported: no uv_async binding and an unsynchronised handle registry; bridges are a future (libuv async) module (one more trampoline type under ADR-0008's rule) or a queue polled from the tick.
Naive purity is allocation-heavy (6,832 B/request measured); the fix (linear mutable accumulator) makes the core pure by contract rather than by construction and needs review discipline.

Wide event alphabet (17 event kinds x ~8 phases) is more code than the equivalent callbacks; unknown-event arms are assertion-violations that must never be reachable in production because a raise inside a parser callback poisons the parser.
Shared tick makes timeouts +/- tick-ms; exact per-connection timers cost 152 B + a callback each (switchable in the shell only).
Data-after-close is a server policy layered over a strict parser; enabling the lenient data-after-close flag would silently change behaviour (kept strict, tested at chunk=1).

Where the obvious alternative (direct callbacks mutating a connection record as in test-echo.sps) is simply better: fewer lines, one fewer layer, no reply/effect split, no interpreter contract to test. Where it is worse: every connection-semantics test needs a socket or a hand-built fake handle, and pause/resume, cap, backpressure and timeout logic interleave with libuv verbs inside callbacks, which is exactly where test-echo.sps needed its own finishing flag and uv-handle-open? guard.

spike.csug_quote: From https://cisco.github.io/ChezScheme/csug10.0/foreign.html, Section 4.4 "Continuations and Foreign Calls" (verbatim): "foreign-callable and foreign-procedure allow arbitrary nesting of foreign and Scheme calls. Because other languages do not support the fully general first-class continuations of Scheme, the interaction between continuations and nested calls among Scheme and foreign procedures is problematic. Chez Scheme handles this interaction in a general manner by trapping attempts to return to stale foreign contexts rather than by restricting the use of continuations directly. A foreign context is a foreign frame and return point corresponding to a particular call from a foreign language, e.g., C, into Scheme. A foreign context becomes stale after a normal return to the context or after a return to some other foreign context beneath it on the control stack. As a result of this treatment, Scheme continuations may be used to throw control either upwards or downwards logically through any mix of Scheme and foreign frames. Furthermore, until some return to a foreign context is actually performed, all return points remain valid. In particular, this means that programs that use continuations exclusively for nonlocal exits never attempt to return to a stale foreign context. (Nonlocal exits themselves are no problem and are implemented by the C library function longjmp or the equivalent.) Programs that use continuations more generally also function properly as long as they never actually return to a stale foreign context, even if control logically moves past stale foreign contexts via invocation of continuations. One implication of this mechanism is that the C stack pointer is not automatically restored to its base value when a continuation is used on the Scheme side to perform a nonlocal exit. If the program continues to run after the nonlocal exit, any further build-up of the C stack will add to the existing build up, which might result in a C stack overflow." Section 4.3 (verbatim): "Mixed use of foreign-callable and foreign-procedure may result in nesting of foreign and Scheme calls, and this results in some interesting considerations when continuations are involved, directly or indirectly (as via the default exception handler). See Section 4.4 for a discussion of the interaction between foreign calls and continuations." On threads (verbatim): "The __collect_safe convention for a callable activates a calling thread if the thread is not already activated, and the thread's activation state is reverted when the callable returns." and "Since active threads operating in C code prevent the storage management system from garbage collecting, a thread should be deactivated via Sdeactivate_thread or through a foreign-procedure __collect_safe declaration whenever the thread may spend a significant amount of time in C code. This is especially important whenever the thread calls a C library function, like read, that may block indefinitely." The chapter contains 0 occurrences of "engine" and 0 of "dynamic-wind" (measured by text search of the fetched page).
conclusions: Scope of every item: Chez Scheme 10.4.1 threaded (tarm64osx), libuv 1.52.1 via chez-libuv v0.5.0, macOS 26.6.2 arm64, measured 2026-09-19.

A continuation captured inside a chez-libuv callback is unusable once that callback has returned: with call/cc the callback body resumes and Chez raises 'attempt to return to stale foreign context' when the trampoline returns to C (E2a/E2b); with call/1cc the body does not resume and Chez raises 'attempt to invoke shot one-shot continuation' (recorded by dispatch-guarded as a pending callback error) followed by the stale-context trap (E1a/E1b). The trap is a bare &assertion that escapes uv-run without &uv-callback-error wrapping because it fires after dispatch-guarded has returned; the process does not crash, a subsequent uv-run works (E2c), and teardown closes the loop.

A callback-captured continuation contains uv-run and the rest of the top-level program: invoking it re-runs everything after uv-run (E1b/E2b printed the post-uv-run line twice; the unguarded E1b looped forever). There is no way to make such a continuation valid; designs must never store-and-invoke them.

The two-level loop works with zero continuation errors: coroutines started from top level, await! capturing with only Scheme frames beneath, callbacks that only enqueue wakeups, a scheduler alternating the ready queue with (uv-run loop 'once); timer, TCP on-data and write-completion wakeups through three nested Scheme frames, and an interleaved second coroutine all verified (E3). Cost: ~30-36 ns per pure suspend/resume (1e6 cycles in 30-36 ms; call/1cc and call/cc indistinguishable, E3b) and ~13 us per cycle when each cycle includes a 0 ms timer plus one uv-run 'once (10,000 cycles: 131-138 ms wall, 17-20 ms CPU).

Engines work as handlers driven from a top-level scheduler and resume correctly after uv-run (E4a); uv-run inside a slice is fine when expiry happens in Scheme (E4b); expiry inside a callback does not stale the foreign frame and the callback completes across 200 resumptions (E4c). However, engine expiry exits uv-run's dynamic-wind, clearing chez-libuv's loop-running flag, so the binding then accepts a nested uv-run that genuinely re-enters libuv's uv_run while the outer one is suspended on the C stack (E4d, 200 nested runs dispatching another timer's callbacks, no crash in 2/2 runs). The re-entry refusal is not a safety net for engine designs; an engine-based design must guarantee no callback ever runs inside a slice.

Cross-thread hand-off via a mutex-protected queue drained by a loop-thread 1 ms timer works (E5a). Calling uv-write! from a non-loop thread corrupts the binding: a single call happened to work twice (E5b), but 2000 concurrent calls produced, across 4 runs, a hang with lost data (gtimeout kill, exit 124), 'invalid memory reference' faults inside uv-run, and registry corruption at teardown ('0 is not of type #<record type registry-entry>') (E5b2). uv_async is not bound, so the polling timer is currently the only wake-up path.

Because uv_run is bound without __collect_safe (native.sls:242), a loop thread blocked in uv-run stalls every other Scheme thread at its next collection until the loop thread re-enters Scheme: a worker's 27 ms allocation loop took 10.27 s under a 300 ms poll timeout and 92 ms under a 1 ms timer (E5c). Thread-offload designs need a short-period timer armed, or the binding needs __collect_safe on uv_run and its callables.

The plain re-entry refusal is exact and synchronous (E6): &uv-invalid-argument, who=uv-run, reason=loop-running, identical for 'nowait/'once/'default, catchable inside the callback with the loop continuing; uv-loop-teardown! from a callback raises the same with who=uv-loop-teardown!.

CSUG foreign.html (csug10.0) says nothing about engines or dynamic-wind in relation to foreign-callable (0 text matches each); its only guidance is the Section 4.4 stale-foreign-context rule and the __collect_safe/thread-activation material, both quoted verbatim in the report.

experiments.name: E1a: call/1cc captured in timer A callback, invoked from timer B callback
experiments.verdict: A's body did not resume; 'attempt to invoke shot one-shot continuation' was recorded as a pending callback error, then 'attempt to return to stale foreign context' escaped uv-run unwrapped; no crash, no hang, teardown closed the loop then re-raised the stored error. Byte-identical across 2 runs.

experiments.name: E1b: call/1cc captured in a callback, invoked from top level after uv-run returned
experiments.verdict: Same two errors as E1a; the post-uv-run top-level line printed twice, proving the continuation carries the rest of the top-level program. An earlier unguarded version re-invoked itself forever (>64 MB output) and had to be capped. Byte-identical across 2 runs.

experiments.name: E2a: full call/cc captured in timer A callback, invoked from timer B callback
experiments.verdict: A's body resumed inside B's dispatch; the trap fired when A's trampoline returned to C; bare &assertion escaped uv-run (after dispatch-guarded returned); teardown ok. Byte-identical across 2 runs. E2b (top-level invocation) and E2c (loop re-run after trap: new timer fired, uv-run #f, teardown ok) behaved consistently.

experiments.name: E3: two-level loop coroutines (timer + TCP on-data wakeups, nested frames, interleaved coroutine, 10k cycles)
experiments.verdict: Works with no continuation errors: handler received hello/world through handle-connection!>recv-message!>recv!>await!, echoed via awaited uv-write!, ticker interleaved 4 sleeps. 10,000 pure cycles 0-2 ms; 10,000 timer+uv-run-once cycles 131-138 ms wall / 17-20 ms CPU. E3b: 1e6 cycles in 30-36 ms => ~33 ns per suspend/resume, call/1cc and call/cc indistinguishable. 2 runs differ only in timings.

experiments.name: E4a/E4b/E4c/E4d: engines as handlers; uv-run inside a slice; expiry inside a callback; nested uv-run while callback suspended
experiments.verdict: E4a: 600 slices, engine resumed correctly after uv-run 'once ran timer callbacks (correct sum). E4b: 300 uv-run 'nowait calls from inside slices, fine. E4c: expiry inside a callback's foreign frame, callback body sliced 200 times then returned normally, no stale-context error. E4d: expiry inside a callback clears chez-libuv's loop-running flag (dynamic-wind after thunk), so a nested uv-run from the expire handler is NOT refused and re-enters libuv's uv_run while the outer one is suspended; it dispatched another timer's callback 3 times; no crash in 2/2 runs but this is a libuv-documented forbidden re-entry. All byte-identical or timing-only differences across 2 runs.

experiments.name: E5a: worker thread -> mutex queue -> 1 ms loop-thread timer -> uv-write! to TCP peer
experiments.verdict: Delivered intact; write completion ran on the loop thread; 0-1 ms hand-off latency. 2 runs differ only in timings (43/47 polls). E5c (same file family, e5c-gc-stall-while-blocked-in-uv-run.sps): a worker's 27 ms allocation loop took 10.27 s while the loop thread blocked in uv-run with a 300 ms timer (34 GCs each waiting for the loop thread to leave C; uv_run is bound without __collect_safe at native.sls:242), 92 ms with a 1 ms timer.

experiments.name: E5b2 (NEGATIVE): worker thread calls uv-write! directly on the loop thread's handle, 2000 concurrent writes each side
experiments.verdict: Undefined behaviour manifested in 4/4 runs, three different ways: hang with lost data and gtimeout kill; memory fault caught inside uv-run; corruption of chez-libuv's unsynchronised registry visible at teardown. (E5b, a single cross-thread uv-write!, happened to work in 2/2 runs -- not evidence of safety.)

experiments.name: E6: (uv-run loop 'nowait) from inside an on-data callback
experiments.verdict: Exact refusal: a single-component &uv-invalid-argument with who=uv-run, reason=loop-running (loop.sls:55-56), identical for all three modes, raised synchronously at the call site so the callback's own guard catches it and the loop continues. Byte-identical across 2 runs.

judges.hybrid: Yes, a hybrid beats every single proposal on this lens: the sans-I/O conn-step core (State x Event -> State x [Action], parser inside via the feed-parser/reply-parser split with run-to-completion) as the connection layer, driven by the two-level scheduler as its shell, with handlers as coroutines started from the scheduler. libuv callbacks only enqueue bytes-arrived/eof/read-error/write-completed/tick into a per-connection inbox and mark it runnable; each scheduler turn drains inboxes through conn-step and executes actions; (uv-run loop 'once) when nothing is runnable; the call-handler action spawns a call/1cc coroutine from a scheduler frame (spike E3's shape) whose direct-style verbs (respond!, sink-write!, body-read!, await, with-deadline) are nothing but events into the core. Result: no application code and no parser callback ever runs under a C frame, so store-and-reraise is reachable only by ten library-owned closures and the E1/E2 question is moot; the socket-free corpus lane (every fixture at every chunk size, LIFO handlers, cap, close, fake-clock timeouts) and the measured head/ready ordering invariant carry over unchanged; handlers get await without the promise Tier 1 stale-context hazard. Take the promise proposal's M1 pause-in-on-body-data protocol (consumed includes the delivered span; re-feed from consumed after parser-resume!) to pin sans-I/O's risk 5, and keep the threads proposal's uv_async/__collect_safe work as an upstream chez-libuv ask for later cross-thread offload, not a v1 dependency. Reject for v1: engines (J1 parser poisoning at every mid-feed preemption), OS-thread handlers (E5b2, E5c, unbound uv_async), callback-captured await (bare &assertion abandoning uv_run C frames on one escaped raise). Required fixes carried in: fulfil! must check state='parked and a cell-parked coroutine must record its cell so inbox wakes and cell fulfilments are mutually exclusive (two-level sketch double-resume hazard); the interpreter's depth counter must wrap drain!, not only parser-feed!; handler deadlines are delivered at the next park (no preemption, same as every non-engine design). The alternative hybrid in the task (callbacks at the connection layer, coroutines only in handlers) is strictly weaker: parser callbacks would still run under C frames and handler coroutines could only be resumed safely if the connection layer also enqueued, at which point it is the two-level shell anyway.

(2) CONNECTION SHELL = direct callbacks (CPS shape), no per-connection coroutine: parse inside on-data with parse-ahead to max-pipeline, callback-pause at on-message-complete for exact boundaries and in on-body-data for the one-slot body mailbox, guarded uv-read-stop!/uv-read-start!, one on-write-done closure per connection carrying sizes in a FIFO, one tick timer + timing wheel per loop, 16 KiB read buffer; idle keep-alive connections then cost ~2 KiB of Scheme and synchronous handlers pay zero scheduler cost. (4) Do NOT take engines' preemption (J1 parser poisoning at slice boundaries, missing uv-run re-guard per E4b/E4d, set-timer conflict) unless a benchmark shows CPU-hog handlers are a real workload; do NOT take promise Tier 1 (4.1 KiB per suspended await, unwrapped escape from uv-run one raise away); do NOT take threads until chez-libuv binds uv_async and rebinds uv_run __collect_safe, after which a worker pool for CPU-bound handlers can sit behind the same command inbox. (5) Operability gates in make test: rg gate that handler-facing libraries export no uv-* names, the phase assertion, a double-close test asserting exactly one on-close, a mutation row removing the guard that must go red, and a pin test for the unexported httparse flag bits (F-CONNECTION-CLOSE = 2). Versus CPS alone: awaiting handlers get direct style and cannot stop the loop. Versus two-level alone: 10k idle connections carry no 35 MB of parked stack segments and no extra hop per delivery. Versus sans-io alone: the 2.5x allocation and per-chunk streaming round trips go away while the pure core and its tests stay.
