As a v1 primary architecture: it is only good after an upstream chez-libuv change that does not exist. With uv_run bound plain (native.sls:242) a worker's allocation stalls until the loop returns to Scheme (spike E5c: 10.27 s vs 27 ms; its own spike A: 3005 ms), so Tier 1 must run a 1 ms heartbeat that imposes a measured 573 us mean / 2.4 ms max response-latency floor and 1% idle CPU; Tier 2 (uv_async 14th trampoline + __collect_safe rebinding of uv_run and all thirteen trampolines) is a chez-libuv v0.6 slice unmeasured on Linux. Independently, a fixed pool of N=cores workers cannot serve 10k concurrent connections whose handlers park on slow clients: max-blocked-writers aborts connections to protect the pool, and Chez has no thread cancel so a wedged handler loses a slot forever and can hang thread-join at shutdown.

none for Tier 0. Tier 1 (await on callback-captured call/1cc) is NOT refuted: my rerun of its await-timer.sps ran 1000 capture-in-A/resume-in-B rounds dry 2/2 under the escape discipline, so spike conclusion 2 ('no way to make it valid') overstates E1a/E2a, which only tested normal return. But its failure mode (any raise reaching the capturing callback's stale dispatch-guarded) is a bare &assertion escaping uv-run that abandons the rest of that loop iteration's callbacks, reachable from handler code one uncaught raise away.

servers.name: h11 (python-hyper/h11)
lessons: Model chez-http-server's connection layer as h11 does: two role-local state automata plus small orthogonal flags (keep-alive, 100-continue-waiting, pending-switch-proposals), joined by explicit event-triggered and state-triggered transition tables (_state.py:196-246) -- this is the missing connection-lifetime layer above chez-httparse's per-message parser state.

Copy the keep-alive latch rule (HTTP/1.0->close, Connection:close->close, one-way latch) almost verbatim, and use it to decide when to stop calling parser-feed! -- this directly resolves the measured chez-httparse close-then-second-message 'error result: after a close-marked message completes, the connection layer must stop feeding rather than expect more input.

Server-side pipelining needs only a pause flag, not a response-reorder queue: stop parsing (don't call parser-feed! again) once the current message is done and bytes remain buffered, resume after the response is fully sent -- FIFO ordering falls out for free. Use chez-httparse's reported consumed byte count to find the pipelining boundary.

Put ALL backpressure (both read-side pause/resume and write-side throttling) in the imperative shell around uv-read-stop!/uv-read-start! and uv-stream-write-queue-size, keeping the parser/state-machine core a pure function of bytes<->events with zero I/O awareness -- exactly h11's split, and a natural fit given chez-libuv's own no-bounded-write-queue design (ADR-0018).

Only a head-of-message incomplete-buffer cap (h11: 16 KiB -> 431) belongs in the connection core; ALL timeouts (header, body, idle-keepalive, lingering-close-drain) must live in the imperative shell via make-uv-timer, since h11 supplies zero timeout logic and zero default numbers for them -- we must choose our own timeout defaults, we cannot copy h11's (it has none).

Track Expect:100-continue as a single boolean outside the formal state machine, cleared on any response or on the client streaming the body anyway -- cheap to add and avoids a handler deadlocking against a client that stopped waiting.

Model CONNECT and Upgrade through one shared pending-proposal/status-code-driven-acceptance code path (101 for Upgrade, 2xx for CONNECT), with 'switch pending' taking priority over 'must close' when both fire together, and hand back unconsumed buffered bytes (h11's trailing_data) to whatever owns the connection after the handoff.

Copy framing precedence exactly, especially two subtle cases likely to be gotten wrong: (a) duplicate-but-IDENTICAL Content-Length values are valid, only a differing duplicate is an error; (b) a second Transfer-Encoding header or a non-chunked T-E value maps to 501 specifically, not to a generic 400 bucket -- our error-mapping table needs this as its own case.

Carry a suggested status code as DATA on parse/policy error conditions (mirroring error_status_hint), and keep 'write the response, then decide to close' as a separate, later, explicit action in the imperative shell -- never let raising the condition itself trigger a response or a close. Also preserve h11's asymmetry that a peer protocol violation must NOT by itself prevent us from still sending a real error response back.

Flag the half-close gap explicitly in the architecture doc: h11/RFC7230 6.6's lingering-close protocol needs a TCP half-close (shutdown-write-only) primitive, and chez-libuv's uv-close! is a whole-handle close with no uv_shutdown binding mentioned as available -- this needs either a documented deviation or a chez-libuv extension, decided consciously rather than by default.

Adopt h11's no-handler-API stance as an architecture decision: the connection-semantics module should expose an h11-like event stream (new-request/header-data/body-data/message-complete/connection-closed, plus the send-side mirror), with a strictly separate module deciding how those events become calls into Scheme handler code -- keeping the two independently testable, as h11's own test-file split proves out.

Plan from day one for a live differential test harness for the connection layer (drive chez-http-server against a real second HTTP/1.1 implementation over a real socket, e.g. curl or Python's http.client/h11-as-client), mirroring test_against_stdlib_http.py and chez-httparse's own llhttp differential discipline -- this is currently a gap in the empty target repo.
servers.limits: Exactly one real limit: DEFAULT_MAX_INCOMPLETE_EVENT_SIZE = 16*1024 (16 KiB) (_connection.py:69, constructor default at :170) -- caps only the buffered-but-not-yet-parseable request/status-line+headers prefix, not body size; enforced in next_event() (_connection.py:484-490), raising RemoteProtocolError(error_status_hint=431) when exceeded. Comment cites precedents: node.js 80KiB, Tomcat 8KiB, IIS 16KiB, Apache ~8KiB/line (_connection.py:64-68). Secondary sanity bound: CONTENT_LENGTH_MAX_DIGITS = 20 (_headers.py:15), rejecting absurd Content-Length numerals (default 400). No limit on header count, URI length, body size, or number of pipelined requests buffered.
servers.timeouts: h11 has ZERO built-in timeouts of any kind -- it is sans-I/O and has no clock/timer. There is no header-read timeout, body-read timeout, idle-connection timeout, or keep-alive timeout anywhere in the source (confirmed by full read of all core files). test_408_request_timeout (tests/test_connection.py:990-994) does NOT test a timeout mechanism; it only proves the server state machine legally permits spontaneously sending Response(status_code=408) from IDLE with no prior Request seen (SERVER: IDLE -> Response -> SEND_BODY, _state.py:208-210) -- detecting that a timeout occurred is entirely external/embedder responsibility, per docs/api.rst:282-286.

servers.name: hyper HTTP/1 server connection-semantics extraction
lessons: Separate the read-buffer-for-headers cap from the write-buffer/backpressure cap - hyper conflates both into one max_buf_size (~408KiB default) which is convenient but couples two independent concerns; given chez-libuv fixes the read buffer at 64KiB/connection and has no bounded write queue at all (ADR-0018), pick two independently-tunable numbers instead.

Model read/write halves as two small closed state machines (Reading: Init/Continue/Body/KeepAlive/Closed; Writing: Init/Body/KeepAlive/Closed) plus a tri-state keep-alive flag (Idle/Busy/Disabled), and only advance to 'ready for next request' when BOTH sides simultaneously reach their KeepAlive sentinel (conn.rs:1093-1112) - a clean 5+4+3-state pattern that answers 'is it safe to read the next head' without scattered booleans.

Copy the close-delimited-forces-close rule verbatim: make 'the response used close-delimited framing' a property the ENCODER exposes, and check it at every site that finalizes a write, not just in the keep-alive decision function, or it's easy to miss a call site and leak a non-reusable connection back into a keep-alive state.

Defer the automatic 100-continue write until the handler has actually expressed interest in the request body (polled it), not merely 'when Expect:100-continue and a body arrive' - replicate hyper's exact test (expect_continue_waits_for_body_poll) to prove a handler that never touches the body never causes a 100-continue to hit the wire.

Express body backpressure in both directions as 'stop pumping the transport', not 'buffer unboundedly': read direction should stop re-arming/continuing libuv reads (or logically not consume the parse buffer) while our request-body consumer's slot is full (hyper's is capacity-exactly-1); write direction should stop pulling more frames from the response body producer once our own outstanding-write-bytes counter (tracked ourselves, per ADR-0018) crosses a chosen watermark, resuming via uv-stream-write-queue-size the way the project brief already prescribes.

Never call the platform close/shutdown primitive while bytes are still buffered for write - assert this explicitly and write hyper's two exact regression tests (flush-before-yield, no-shutdown-while-buffered) against our own dispatch loop once it exists, since both were subtle interleavings easy to reintroduce when an 'early exit/yield' fast path gets added later. Additionally, unlike hyper (which never owns a raw closeable handle with a double-close hazard and therefore needs no guard), we MUST add an explicit single-owner close-once guard at the boundary between our connection state machine and chez-libuv's uv-close!, since a second uv-close! silently discards the on-close callback (ADR-0007) - this is a gap hyper's design doesn't have to solve and offers no pattern for.

Treat clean EOF with no partially-read request as ordinary teardown (not an error) for a server, but EOF with a partial request in flight as an error - a single boolean ('do we have a partially-consumed request') implements this asymmetry cleanly and avoids noisy error logging for the common 'client done with a keep-alive connection' case.

Reject Transfer-Encoding + Content-Length together outright (400 + close) rather than copying hyper's more lenient 'TE wins, CL dropped, just force close' - hyper's own in-code comment admits the strict RFC7230 reading is 'MUST respond 400 and close'; given request smuggling risk and no backward-compat burden, be stricter than hyper here.

Decide explicitly, and document, what we auto-generate on error versus hyper's minimal set (only 400/414/431 auto-generated; 408 and 500 are NEVER auto-sent by hyper, connections are simply dropped) - if chez-http-server wants to be friendlier (auto-408 on header timeout, auto-500 on an uncaught handler condition), that is a deliberate, documented deviation from the reference, not something to inherit silently by omission.

Build the first cut of chez-http-server's dispatcher as strictly one-request-in-flight-per-connection, exactly like hyper - pipelining support should mean read-ahead-plus-flush-batching only, never concurrent handler execution on one connection; treat true per-connection request concurrency as a separate, harder feature to consider later, not something to bolt onto the basic loop from day one.
servers.limits: All defaults, with file:line, tabulated in report §7. Headline numbers: INIT_BUFFER_SIZE=8192B (io.rs:15); MINIMUM_MAX_BUFFER_SIZE=8192B floor for Builder::max_buf_size, panics below it (io.rs:18, http1.rs:381-387); DEFAULT_MAX_BUFFER_SIZE=8192+4096*100=417792B (~408KiB, io.rs:23) - shared ceiling for BOTH header-parse read buffer (exceeding => Error::TooLarge=>431) AND response write buffer backpressure; MAX_BUF_LIST_BUFFERS=16 distinct queued Bufs before forced flush (io.rs:30); MAX_WRITEV_BUFS=64 iovecs per writev syscall (io.rs:281); DEFAULT_MAX_HEADERS=100 header slots, Builder::max_headers overridable, exceeding => 431 (role.rs:31); MAX_URI_LEN=65534B (u16::MAX-1), exceeding => 414 URI Too Long (role.rs:34, test http_11_uri_too_long tests_server.rs:1188-1203); CHUNKED_EXTENSIONS_LIMIT=16384B whole-body total (decode.rs:20); TRAILER_LIMIT=16384B whole-body total, marked TODO to become configurable (decode.rs:25); poll_loop fairness cap = 16 pipelined iterations per wakeup before yield (dispatch.rs:172), not a wall-clock limit. No max-request-body-size limit, no response-write timeout, no idle-connection timeout beyond what header_read_timeout incidentally provides between messages - all left to the application. Full table: report §7.
servers.timeouts: Only ONE built-in timeout exists in hyper's H1 server layer: h1_header_read_timeout, default 30 seconds (Dur::Default(Some(Duration::from_secs(30))), http1.rs:250), and it is INERT unless the caller also supplies a Timer via Builder::timer() (no timer configured => effectively unbounded header-read wait, confirmed by http1.rs doc: "Requires a Timer ... Panics if configured without a Timer" only fires when set; otherwise it's simply never armed since Time::Empty is the default, http1.rs:74,244). It resets per message and, because it's the ONLY timer, also functions as the de facto idle-keep-alive timeout between pipelined/successive messages on the same connection - proven by test name+body header_read_timeout_as_idle_timeout (tests_server.rs:1656-1697), which is literally testing that the next request's header-read clock (not a separate idle timer) kills a quiet keep-alive connection. On timeout: poll_read_head returns Error::new_header_timeout() directly (conn.rs:260-265) WITHOUT going through the parse-error/on_error->auto-response path - so a header-read timeout closes the socket with NO bytes written (no 408 response). There is no request-body-read timeout, no response-write timeout, and no distinct post-handshake idle timeout in this crate; all are left to the application (e.g., race the handler future or wrap the body against an external timer). Full detail: report §7, §11.

servers.name: Go net/http server (server.go, transfer.go, request.go)
servers.license: BSD-3-Clause ("Copyright 2009 The Go Authors. All rights reserved.")
lessons: Serialize strictly one request per connection (read, handle, write, then read next) rather than building any pipelining/reordering layer — this also naturally avoids chez-httparse's measured close-marked-message-then-error quirk, since you'd never feed a second message after a close-marked one anyway.

Default to unlimited body/idle read/write timeouts like Go does, but bound header size by default (Go's only non-zero timeout-adjacent default) — and document the unlimited defaults loudly given they're a known Go production footgun (slowloris-class risk).

Centralize Content-Length/Transfer-Encoding precedence in one pure function shared by request and response paths, mirroring fixLength's precedence order (TE beats CL; differing duplicate CLs are a hard error; identical duplicates dedupe; 1xx/204/304/HEAD force zero-length) — a natural fit for the functional-core mandate.
Reject non-'chunked' or multi-valued Transfer-Encoding strictly and map it to 501 (never 400), and never echo the rejected value back into the response body (XSS hardening Go applies deliberately).

Body-size limiting should be an explicit, composable opt-in (MaxBytesReader-equivalent) rather than parser/connection-layer behavior, but consider giving chez-http-server a default cap (with a real 413) since we lack Go's mature ecosystem of handler-level conventions yet.

Default to half-duplex request/response handling (don't start writing the response before the request body is consumed or explicitly abandoned) to avoid the Issue-15527-class deadlock, with a bounded drain-then-close fallback around ~256KiB matching maxPostHandlerReadBytes.

Reserve a lingering half-close-then-delay-then-close specifically for the two 'we unilaterally stopped reading a body the client might still be sending' scenarios (header-too-large, body-limit-hit); use an immediate close everywhere else. Note chez-libuv v0.5 has no uv_shutdown/half-close binding, so this may need either a chez-libuv feature addition or a pragmatic Go-style flat-sleep-then-full-close substitute.

Only propagate connection-cancellation from genuine on-error/EOF callbacks, never from 'more bytes arrived early on this connection' — directly avoids the pipelining/CloseNotify false-positive Go fixed in 1.11 and regression-tests.

Treat Go's negative-space findings (no 408, no server-side ExpectContinueTimeout, no built-in CONNECT/Upgrade handling) as legitimate design choices worth recording as our own ADRs, not gaps to silently fill.

Port TestServerValidatesHostHeader's full case table and the TestUnsupportedTransferEncodingsReturn501 / TestInvalidChunkedBodies / TestCloseNotifierPipelined tests early as our highest-value conformance regression tests, since each encodes a previously real-world-debated bug (Go issues 3595, 11549, 12027, 12785, 14940, 15527, 16490, 22682, 23921, 31753, 36381 are all cited in the source comments).
servers.limits: DefaultMaxHeaderBytes=1<<20 (1 MiB, server.go:939); DefaultMaxHeaderValueCount=500 (server.go:944); initialReadLimitSize=maxHeaderBytes+4096 'bufio slop' (server.go:960-962); maxPostHandlerReadBytes=256<<10=262144 (server.go:1164); bufferBeforeChunkingSize=2048 (server.go:342); conn.bufw size=4096 (server.go:2036); copyBufPoolSize=32768 (server.go:876); rstAvoidanceDelay=500ms (server.go:1806); shutdownPollIntervalMax=500ms (server.go:3227). Body size itself is uncapped by default at the connection layer (opt-in via MaxBytesReader).
servers.timeouts: Server.ReadTimeout, ReadHeaderTimeout (falls back to ReadTimeout), WriteTimeout, and IdleTimeout (falls back to ReadTimeout) all default to 0 = unlimited (server.go:3062-3091,3745-3757) — only header-size/value-count have non-zero defaults. TLS handshake timeout is derived as the min of any positive ReadHeaderTimeout/ReadTimeout/WriteTimeout, else unlimited (server.go:964-984). No 408 status and no server-side ExpectContinueTimeout exist (confirmed absent by grep).

servers.name: Node.js http.Server (llhttp-based)
servers.license: MIT-style permission notice (Joyent copyright) in every core file header; Node.js project overall is MIT licensed.
lessons: Compute keep-alive once, inside the message-complete callback, from parser flags read at that moment (version + connection-close/keep-alive flags + does-framing-need-EOF); never re-read parser flags later since chez-httparse resets them between pipelined messages.

Model pipelining as two decoupled queues: an incoming[] queue the parser keeps filling regardless of response state, and an outgoing[] FIFO where only one response is ever attached to the connection's write side at a time; advance it only when the current response's write-completion (uv-write! callback) fires, not when its handler returns.

Track outstanding queued-response bytes ourselves at the connection level and call uv-read-stop! when they cross a threshold, uv-read-start! again once they drain back down -- this is the direct answer to chez-libuv having no bounded write queue in the binding.

Make every framework-synthesized error response Connection-close, and never attempt to write one once any response bytes have already gone out for that request -- check for already-sent headers before ever trying a synthetic error write.

Collapse all definitely-unparseable requests into one generic 400 rather than trying to distinguish 501 vs 505 vs 400 from parser error codes; reserve distinct codes (431, 413, 408) for cases with genuinely different client-actionable meaning.
Implement maxRequestsPerSocket as a graceful two-step wind-down (advertise Connection: close on the last allowed response, then 503 the next one) rather than an abrupt mid-limit disconnect.

Treat Expect:100-continue handling and keep-alive-reuse eligibility as needing a SINGLE source-of-truth state transition, not two independently-triggered listeners racing each other -- Node's own historical bug here (test-http-expect-continue-reuse-race.js) is exactly the failure mode to avoid.
Expose close as three separately callable operations -- close-gracefully (stop accepting, only reap idle), close-idle-only, and close-all-forcefully -- rather than one shutdown verb with a flag.

Make the on-close callback the single unconditional cleanup point for a connection: abort every still-pending request/response object there, regardless of which error path led to the close, mirroring chez-libuv's rule that a server must own every close initiation.

Plan upgrade/CONNECT as two sub-cases from the start: request-already-complete (hand over the raw connection immediately) vs request-body-still-streaming (need a wrapper that defers raw post-body bytes until chez-httparse's on-headers-complete/skip-body plus body-completion has actually finished).

Default behavior for an unrecognized Upgrade: header with no registered interest should be 'treat as a normal request', not 'reject' -- only CONNECT and an accepted-but-unhandled Upgrade should hard-close.

Maintain two membership views of live connections -- 'idle, never mid-message' and 'active, currently mid-message' -- as cheaply updatable sets, to make an idle-only close operation O(idle-count) instead of a full scan.
servers.limits: maxHeaderSize / http.maxHeaderSize / --max-http-header-size: default 16384 bytes (16 KiB) total header bytes (src/node_options.h:186; doc/api/http.md:4009-4021); overflow -> HPE_HEADER_OVERFLOW -> 431. server.maxHeadersCount: default 1000 header pairs (2000 field+value slots internally, MAX_HEADER_PAIRS in lib/_http_common.js:53); overflow -> HPE_HEADER_OVERFLOW -> 431 (counted in C++ TrackHeaderPair, src/node_http_parser.cc:1042-1067). Chunk-extension size cap: hardcoded 16384 bytes, NOT configurable (kMaxChunkExtensionsSize, src/node_http_parser.cc:86); overflow -> HPE_CHUNK_EXTENSIONS_OVERFLOW -> 413. server.maxRequestsPerSocket: default 0 (no limit); when reached, response gets forced Connection: close; a request arriving after the limit gets 503 plus a 'dropRequest' event.
servers.timeouts: server.requestTimeout: default 300000 ms (5 min), governs the entire request receive window (lib/_http_server.js:555-561). server.headersTimeout: default min(60000, requestTimeout) ms, must be <= requestTimeout or ERR_OUT_OF_RANGE is thrown at construction (lines 563-573). server.keepAliveTimeout: default 65000 ms in this pinned commit (lines 575-581) -- NOTE this pinned commit's doc has a REPLACEME changelog entry raising the default from 5000ms to 65000ms, meaning 65000ms is an UNRELEASED change on Node main as of this fetch; all currently-released Node versions default to 5000 ms. Flag this explicitly when citing. server.keepAliveTimeoutBuffer: default 1000 ms, added on top of keepAliveTimeout when arming the post-response socket timer (actual socket timeout = keepAliveTimeout + keepAliveTimeoutBuffer). server.connectionsCheckingInterval: default 30000 ms, sweep interval for expiring headers/request-timeout connections via an unref'd setInterval. server.timeout (idle-socket timeout covering all traffic): default 0 (disabled). Every timeout, once fired, maps to the same 408 Request Timeout + Connection: close canned response via socketOnError, sharing the same code path as parse errors.

servers.name: h2o
servers.license: MIT (per copyright/permission header in lib/http1.c and lib/common/socket.c)
lessons: Single-request-in-flight per connection is sufficient for correct pipelining -- no response-reordering queue needed; just don't restart uv-read-start! for request N+1 until request N's response uv-write! has completed.

Backpressure on both directions should be 'one fragment outstanding, stop reading/writing until explicitly acknowledged', not a byte-counted queue -- matches chez-libuv's own no-bounded-write-queue design (ADR-0018) and gives us a natural place to enforce a single-write-in-flight-per-connection discipline the way h2o asserts sock->_cb.write==NULL.

Copy h2o's Content-Length-vs-Transfer-Encoding precedence rule (TE wins when both present) but do NOT copy its silent acceptance of duplicate/conflicting Content-Length headers or of the CL+TE combination -- reject both per RFC 9112 6.3's stricter guidance, since h2o's own code has a known smuggling gap here.

The 'steal the socket, hand back a byte-offset into what's already buffered' pattern (h2o_http1_upgrade / on_upgrade_complete) is the right shape for our own Upgrade/CONNECT hand-off given chez-libuv's explicit, non-GC-driven uv-close! model.

Add an explicit chunk-framing-overhead DoS guard (h2o borrows this from picohttpparser: >=100KiB overhead AND payload <25% of bytes read) at our connection layer -- passing llhttp conformance fixtures proves correctness, not abuse-resistance, and nothing in the PROJECT CONTEXT suggests chez-httparse already has this.

h2o deliberately never sends 408/431/501/505 -- idle/header timeouts just close the TCP connection silently, oversized headers get 400 not 431, and there's no HTTP-version validation. This is a legitimate security-conscious default but a genuine gap, not an oversight; decide consciously whether chez-http-server matches h2o's terse silence or sends informative status lines, and if we do add them, still always close afterward the way h2o closes on every single one of its own error paths.

100-continue should be sent eagerly/unconditionally in origin-server mode with no handler-pre-approval hook for v1 -- this is h2o's real, shipped simplification and RFC 7231 5.1.1 explicitly permits it.

No lingering close is a real, named gap in h2o (an explicit TODO in its source), not something to copy blindly -- chez-libuv's explicit uv-close! model gives us a natural place to add a proper drain/lingering-close policy h2o itself lacks; make this an explicit ADR either way.

Graceful shutdown works best as two independent, composable mechanisms: (a) a lazily-checked flag that forces Connection:close on the NEXT parsed request per connection so in-flight work always completes, and (b) a separately-invoked sweep that force-closes only genuinely IDLE connections (nothing buffered) without waiting out their full idle timeout.

Track a three-state IDLE/ACTIVE/SHUTDOWN tag per connection from the start (cheap, and it's what makes both graceful shutdown and future idle-connection metrics tractable) rather than retrofitting it later.

h2o's HTTP/1 keep-alive idle timeout and header-read timeout are the SAME 10s value by default (req_timeout reused for both) -- decide explicitly whether chez-http-server wants a distinct, likely longer, idle-between-requests timeout rather than silently inheriting a single value for both purposes.

servers.name: nginx
servers.license: 2-clause BSD (nginx's own license, distinct from our target's BSD-3-Clause)
lessons: Keepalive must be a 3-layer decision (version+Connection-token default, post-routing config vetoes, framing-forced veto when body length is unknown and can't be chunked) -- read chez-httparse's F-CONNECTION-* flags inside the header-parse callback per its own documented reset-zeroing warning.

Pipelining must be structurally serial (never concurrent request processing on one connection), which sidesteps response-ordering entirely and matches chez-libuv's single-callback-per-loop-thread model; combined with chez-httparse's measured 'data after close' error, our connection layer -- not the parser -- must stop feeding further requests once a message is close-marked.
Use a posted-work/re-entry pattern instead of direct recursion when immediately continuing to a pipelined next request, to bound stack depth on long pipelines.

Backpressure in both directions should mean 'stop touching the transport, let the reactor resume us' -- map directly onto chez-libuv's uv-read-stop!/uv-read-start! for request-body reads and uv-stream-write-queue-size polling for response writes, never an unbounded internal buffer.

Adopt independent per-phase idle timeouts (header-read, body-read, send, keepalive-idle, keepalive-total-age, keepalive-request-count) with real numeric defaults from day one, not a single global deadline -- gives much better diagnostics and chez-libuv timers are cheap.

Enforce the close-delimited-response rule (unknown-length body + no chunking => must close) as an automatic side effect of the framing/response-header layer, never something a handler has to remember to request.
Decide explicitly on 431 vs nginx's legacy 400-for-header-too-large -- nginx is a historical-accident precedent here, not a spec-conformance one; prefer real 431.

Model lingering close as an explicit small state machine (open->draining->closing->closed) with half-close (FIN via shutdown-write) before final close, nested idle/wall-clock timers, and exactly one uv-close! initiation per handle -- critical given chez-libuv's ADR-0007 rule that a second uv-close! on a closing handle silently discards its callback.

Route the 100-continue response through the normal backpressure-aware write path rather than nginx's unchecked blocking send() shortcut; latch expect-tested state before any size-based pre-rejection so we never invite a body we're about to reject.

Classify request headers explicitly into 'reject duplicates' (Host, Content-Length, Transfer-Encoding, Expect, conditional-request headers, Authorization) vs 'duplicates allowed' (Connection, Cookie, Accept-Encoding, User-Agent) rather than picking one blanket policy.

Design Upgrade/CONNECT as an explicit out-of-band connection-mode transition (stop HTTP framing, become raw relay) separate from the keepalive/pipelining state machine, not a degenerate case woven into it.

Actively manage idle-connection memory: chez-libuv commits a 64KiB foreign read buffer per uv-read-start!, far larger than nginx's ~1KB idle footprint, so consider uv-read-stop! between keepalive requests (trading a syscall for memory) as a deliberate, probably ADR-worthy design decision.

Offer an explicit body-read opt-in (a post-handler continuation invoked once the app asks for the body) rather than eager pre-read, mirroring both nginx's ngx_http_read_client_request_body and chez-httparse's callback shape, while keeping a lower-level streaming mode available for proxy-style use cases.

servers.name: Warp (yesodweb/wai)
servers.license: MIT (per repo LICENSE); note wai/warp specifically, not chez-http-server's own BSD-3-Clause
lessons: Copy the keep-alive truth table (checkReqConnectionHeader + needsChunked + isKeepAlive) and its test-as-truth-table shape (ConnectionSpec.hs) directly — it's small, exhaustive, and normative.

Warp's single-thread-per-connection blocking-IO model gives it backpressure and pipelining-ordering 'for free'; since we're event-loop/callback-driven via chez-libuv (not one-thread-per-connection), we must design an EXPLICIT pull gate for request-body delivery (only feed parser/deliver-to-handler bytes the handler has asked for, buffering the rest, honoring uv-read-stop!/uv-read-start! as our backpressure verbs since libuv has no bounded write queue per ADR-0018) and an explicit backpressure watch on uv-stream-write-queue-size for response streaming, since we don't get blocking-syscall backpressure for free the way Warp does.

For timer economy: copy the CLASSIC pre-rewrite Warp design (tag warp-3.2.28, System.TimeManager.hs) not current master's design — a single shared uv-timer (one FFI timer handle for the WHOLE SERVER) sweeping a plain registry of lightweight per-connection cells with an Active/Inactive/Paused/Canceled state, where tickle/pause/resume are O(1) mutations with zero FFI/timer-heap interaction. This directly sidesteps chez-libuv's one-make-uv-timer-per-connection cost. Accept the tradeoff: firing resolution is 1x-2x the sweep interval, not a precise per-connection deadline.

Copy the pause-timeout-around-I/O-only discipline exactly (Warp: T.pause before calling the handler, T.resume around each body-pull and each response-write, T.tickle on completion) — this is backend-agnostic and composes with whatever concrete timer primitive we choose.

We should be STRICTER than Warp on framing-ambiguity/smuggling: reject duplicate conflicting Content-Length and reject Content-Length+Transfer-Encoding-chunked together rather than silently last-value-wins like Warp's indexRequestHeader fold; chez-httparse/llhttp conformance likely already buys us this if we don't discard the strictness at our connection layer above the parser.

Do not silently coerce unrecognized HTTP major/minor versions the way Warp's httpVersion does (RequestHeader.hs:109-116, defaults anything unrecognized to HTTP/1.0) — decide explicitly whether to reject with 505 or otherwise, and make sure chez-httparse's own version validation isn't discarded by our connection layer.

Send 431 for oversized headers ourselves (a genuine RFC 6585 fit) rather than copy Warp's own inconsistency of resolving its OverLargeHeader exception to 400 despite Settings.hs's doc comment implying 431 — this is a confirmed doc/behavior mismatch in Warp itself, not something to emulate.

Copy the asymmetric close policy: protocol/parse-level errors always close the connection (we no longer trust our position in the byte stream); a well-formed-request-but-handler-threw error MAY keep-alive if we choose (Warp does, via a returned persistence flag threaded through the error-response path).

Copy the 'count the resource at acquisition, not at consumer-thread-start' lesson from Warp's graceful-shutdown accept-race fix (increment the open-connection counter in the accept loop itself, before forking/dispatching) — directly relevant to any accept-then-enqueue-then-process design we build over libuv's on-connection callback.

Keep Upgrade/CONNECT entirely out of the connection-core's vocabulary: expose one primitive equivalent to responseRaw (hand the handler raw send/recv and let it fully own the bytes from then on, unconditionally forcing non-keep-alive/non-return-to-loop), and let application code decide when to invoke it. Do not build any Upgrade-header or CONNECT-method-aware logic into chez-http-server's core loop.

Body-size limiting is a conscious omission in Warp (no hard cap on requestBody consumption, only a bounded UNREAD-body drain budget on keep-alive reuse) — decide explicitly whether chez-http-server enforces a hard body-size cap at the connection layer (recommended, given we're not blocking-IO-backpressure-protected the way Warp is) rather than silently omitting it the way Warp does.

When porting any numeric default/limit, copy the LITERAL constant and verify it against test behavior, not the adjacent doc comment — settingsMaxBuilderResponseBufferSize's doc says '1 MiB' but the actual value is ~1.05 GB, a confirmed 1000x doc/code mismatch caught only by reading the literal directly.

servers.timeouts: settingsTimeout=30 seconds (single shared idle-timeout per connection, guards header read + active body read + response write, converted to microseconds and fed to the timeout manager at Run.hs:299-306; NOT wall-clock-since-connect, paused around app computation via T.pause/T.resume bracketing at every I/O boundary, see report §12). settingsGracefulShutdownTimeout=Nothing (unbounded wait for open-connection counter to hit 0 during shutdown; STM retry-based, no polling). settingsGracefulCloseTimeout1=0 ms for HTTP/1.x (0 = plain immediate close(), NOT lingering-close by default) vs settingsGracefulCloseTimeout2=2000 ms for HTTP/2 (gracefulClose: sends FIN via shutdown(SHUT_WR), reads-and-discards until peer FIN or this timeout, then closes regardless). Timeout manager design: current master delegates entirely to GHC's own per-capability TimerManager (time-manager/System/TimeManager.hs, NOT portable/relevant to us, analogous to "just use libuv's timer heap directly per connection"). The design actually relevant to the task's "one thread, tickle-able handle" framing is the PRE-rewrite implementation still readable at tag warp-3.2.28 (commit d487668804d7a71606d137df3c6d3d1cc359660b): a single Control.Reaper thread sweeping a plain list of {IORef action, IORef state<Active|Inactive|Paused|Canceled>} handles once every `timeout` interval; tickle/resume/pause/cancel are all O(1) lock-free IORef writes with ZERO interaction with any timer/heap structure — this is the timer-economy pattern directly transferable to our single-uv-timer-sweeping-a-hashtable design, sidestepping one-uv-timer-per-connection entirely. Firing resolution is between 1x and 2x the timeout interval (a handle must be tickled at least once per sweep, not have a precise per-tickle deadline).

servers.name: Racket web-server (racket/web-server)
servers.license: MIT/Apache-2.0 dual license (Racket standard package license)
lessons: Copy the keep-alive rule (HTTP/1.1 persistent by default, HTTP/1.0 non-persistent by default, Connection:close forces non-persistent either way) but tokenize the Connection header on commas rather than substring-matching close the way Racket does.

Make 'unterminated body + persistent connection' structurally unreachable in the response writer, as Racket does by forcing chunked framing whenever Content-Length is unknown and the connection isn't already closing.

Reject (400) requests with both Transfer-Encoding:chunked and a Content-Length, or duplicate Content-Length values, rather than silently preferring the first header the way Racket's reference does -- this is a real, traced request-smuggling-shaped gap in the implementation, not a pattern to imitate. Also reject/normalize non-exact Transfer-Encoding values instead of silently falling back to non-chunked.
Bake 1xx/204/304 body suppression into the transport-level response writer itself; Racket leaves this entirely to application authors with no framework guard at all.

Design our own parse/limit-violation-to-HTTP-status mapping (400/408/413/431/505) as a deliberate improvement -- Racket's reference maps every protocol error and every uncaught handler exception to the same outcome: silently killing the connection with no response. Do keep its idea of a pure-logging exception classifier (ECONNRESET/EPIPE/already-closed-port/EOF-at-next-pipelined-request = expected, don't log) as a reusable list.

Reuse the single-timer-manager-thread design (one thread owns all deadlines, blocks on one alarm event plus a message inbox) mapped onto chez-libuv's per-connection uv-timer handles, and reuse its exact five-point reset schedule: on accept, on request data arrival, before the handler runs, after the handler returns a response, and on every outbound chunk/progress event.

Do not rely on an unbounded pipe for the chunked-response producer/drainer split the way Racket does (backpressure there only arrives indirectly once the real-socket write blocks); since chez-libuv has no bounded write queue either (ADR-0018) and only exposes uv-stream-write-queue-size as a congestion signal, our chunked writer must poll/track that explicitly rather than assume Racket's synchronous-port-write backpressure chain.

On a mid-chunked-stream handler error, close the connection abruptly and deliberately withhold the terminating 0\r\n\r\n chunk, exactly as Racket does (citing racket/web-server#93) -- this correctly signals an incomplete response instead of a false success.

Copy the two-call graceful-shutdown state machine (first call: stop accepting, wait up to a grace period, then force; second call, or no grace period configured: immediate force) -- but note Racket has no lingering-close/half-close protocol to copy; that would need to be designed fresh.

Copy the request?->response? handler shape with a response record split into immediately-decided status/headers data plus a single deferred body-writer closure, adapted from the raw connection?/request?->any dispatcher signature.

Copy the test-suite architecture wholesale: fixture-file-per-edge-case parser unit tests, a buffered-pipe harness for asserting exact on-the-wire chunk bytes in response-writer tests, and a real-socket e2e suite per behavior (head, graceful-shutdown, max-concurrent, read-write/slow-loris, etc.) built on a shared (get-port,get-stop) harness -- the slow-loris read-timeout test in particular is the best concrete template for validating our own request-read-timeout.

Consciously decide about, rather than silently inherit, the gaps found: no Expect:100-continue, no Upgrade/CONNECT/WebSocket support in the transport, no HTTP trailers on chunked bodies, and strictly one-request-in-flight-per-connection pipelining (chez-httparse's consumed-byte-count-per-parser-feed! already gives us room to do more here if desired).
